q: A continuous spectrum, unlike a line spectrum, contains:
o: All wavelengths over a range, with no gaps
Only dark lines with no bright background
x: A continuous spectrum spreads smoothly over all wavelengths in a range, like that of a hot filament. A line spectrum shows only certain sharp wavelengths.

q: According to Bohr's model of the hydrogen atom, an electron moving in one of the allowed orbits:
o: Emits a photon on every revolution
x: Bohr postulated stationary orbits in which the electron does not radiate. It emits or absorbs energy only when it jumps between orbits.

q: The ground state of an atom is:
o: The state in which it has been ionised
Any state with energy above zero
The highest energy level an electron can reach
x: The ground state (n = 1 for hydrogen) is the lowest energy level. Higher levels are excited states, and removing the electron is ionisation.

q: The ground-state energy of hydrogen is −13.6 eV and the level energies vary as 1/n². What is the energy of the electron in the fourth orbit (n = 4)?
x: E₄ = −13.6/4² = −13.6/16 = −0.85 eV. Dividing by 4 instead of 16 gives −3.4 eV, which is really the n = 2 level.

q: In hydrogen the n = 3 level is at −1.51 eV and the n = 2 level is at −3.4 eV. An electron dropping from n = 3 to n = 2 emits a photon of energy:
x: Photon energy = E₃ − E₂ = −1.51 − (−3.4) = 1.89 eV. This is the red Balmer line; adding the magnitudes (4.91 eV) is a sign error.

q: The lines of the Brackett series of hydrogen are produced by transitions that end on the level:
x: Lyman ends on n = 1, Balmer on n = 2, Paschen on n = 3, Brackett on n = 4 and Pfund on n = 5.

q: A hydrogen electron is in the n = 2 level, of energy −3.4 eV. The minimum energy needed to free it from the atom is:
x: To free the electron its energy must be raised to zero, so it needs 0 − (−3.4) = 3.4 eV. 13.6 eV applies only to an electron in the ground state.

q: All the lines of the Balmer series are produced by transitions ending at:
x: Every Balmer line comes from an electron falling from a higher level (n = 3, 4, 5 …) down to n = 2.

q: The series limit, the shortest-wavelength line of the Balmer series, corresponds to the transition:
x: The largest energy drop within the Balmer series is from n = ∞ to n = 2, giving the shortest wavelength. n = ∞ to n = 1 is the Lyman series limit.

q: Using 1/λ = R(1/1² − 1/2²) with R = 1.1 × 10⁷ m⁻¹, the wavelength of the first Lyman line of hydrogen is about:
x: 1/λ = 1.1 × 10⁷ × 3/4, so λ = 4/(3.3 × 10⁷) ≈ 1.21 × 10⁻⁷ m = 121 nm. 91 nm is the Lyman series limit and 656 nm is the first Balmer line.

q: White light passes through cool hydrogen gas at room temperature. The absorption lines seen belong almost entirely to the Lyman series because:
o: Lyman lines are the only lines in the visible region
Only electrons in n = 2 can absorb light
Nearly all the atoms are in the ground state, n = 1
Cool atoms can only emit, not absorb, photons
x: At room temperature almost every hydrogen atom is in n = 1, so absorption starts from that level, giving Lyman lines (in the ultraviolet).

q: Compared with the photon from the n = 3 → n = 2 transition in hydrogen, the photon from the n = 4 → n = 2 transition has:
o: The same energy, since both end on n = 2
x: The drop from n = 4 is larger than from n = 3, so the photon has more energy; since E = hc/λ, its wavelength is shorter.

q: Hydrogen atoms excited to the fourth energy level fall back to the ground state by every possible route. The total number of distinct spectral lines possible is:
x: Number of lines = n(n − 1)/2 = 4 × 3/2 = 6: transitions 4→3, 4→2, 4→1, 3→2, 3→1 and 2→1.

q: As the quantum number n increases, the energy levels of the hydrogen atom:
o: Get farther apart and approach zero energy
Get closer together and approach zero energy
Get closer together and approach −13.6 eV
x: Eₙ = −13.6/n² eV, so the gaps between successive levels shrink as n grows and the levels crowd towards 0 eV, the ionisation limit.

q: Which of these sources gives a bright-line emission spectrum?
o: The glowing filament of a tungsten lamp
Neon gas glowing in a discharge tube
x: A low-pressure gas of separate atoms, excited electrically, emits only its own characteristic wavelengths. Hot solids and liquids give continuous spectra.

q: A photon of energy 15 eV is absorbed by a hydrogen atom in its ground state (−13.6 eV). What happens?
o: The atom is ionised and the electron leaves with 1.4 eV of kinetic energy
The electron rises to the n = 2 level
The photon cannot be absorbed because 15 eV matches no level difference
The electron rises to n = 3 and keeps 1.4 eV
x: 15 eV is more than the 13.6 eV ionisation energy, so the electron is freed; the extra 15 − 13.6 = 1.4 eV becomes its kinetic energy. Above ionisation, any photon energy can be absorbed.

q: An atom emits a spectral line of wavelength 600 nm. What is the energy difference between the two levels involved? (h = 6.6 × 10⁻³⁴ J s, c = 3 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹)
x: ΔE = hc/λ = (1.98 × 10⁻²⁵)/(6 × 10⁻⁷) = 3.3 × 10⁻¹⁹ J. Leaving λ in nm gives the 10⁻²⁸ value.

q: In Bohr's model, the angular momentum of the electron in the nth allowed orbit is:
x: Bohr's quantisation condition is mvr = nh/2π, so only orbits with angular momentum a whole multiple of h/2π are allowed.
